title: Klieg Light
subtitle: Los Angeles, Twelve Days in the Autumn of 1947

listing.title: Klieg Light 🎬
listing.blurb: Los Angeles, September 1947. A contract actress at Castellane Pictures has been missing for nine days, the studio's fixer wants her found before the papers notice, and the House committee is serving subpoenas up and down Hollywood. Follow her from a Bunker Hill rooming house to a dead man's swimming pool, a card room on the Sunset Strip and the orange groves of the Valley, to a premiere where every searchlight in town is pointed at the truth. Levels 2–6.

synopsis: Los Angeles in the autumn of 1947 is a boom town that has not decided what it wants to be. A million veterans and their families need houses, the San Fernando Valley is still orange groves and dust, the Red Cars still run to the sea, and the picture business, which had its best year ever in 1946, has just found out that its best year is over. In Washington the House committee investigating un-American activities has announced public hearings on Hollywood for October, and its investigators are in town serving subpoenas and collecting names. On Monday 22 September, Harlan Shay, the man who makes problems go away for Castellane Pictures, a mid-sized studio on Santa Monica Boulevard, hires the party to find Vivian Lark, a twenty-four-year-old contract actress who walked off the lot nine days ago and has not been seen since. Her first starring picture, The Gilded Hour, premieres on Hollywood Boulevard in twelve days. Shay says she is a frightened girl who has run off with a man. He is lying. Vivian ran because she stole a green ledger and an envelope of negatives from the safe of Club Sirocco on the Sunset Strip, and they prove that studio money has been buying votes on the city council for a land syndicate in the West Valley that needs the city's water mains run out to three thousand acres of orange groves. The vote is on 7 October. One councilman who refused the money is already dead. Over four cases, the party finds the actress in a room above the Santa Monica carousel, finds her friend the screenwriter Abel Kurland face down in his own pool the next morning, follows the money from the card room on the Strip to a wrecking yard in Van Nuys and an orange grove that was taken from the family who planted it, and arrives at the premiere of The Gilded Hour knowing that a professional killer will be standing somewhere in the glare of the searchlights. At the end the party holds the green ledger, the negatives and the name of the man who let Abel Kurland drown, and the city, the studio, the committee and the newspapers all want it. What the party does with it is the ending.
hook: Monday 22 September 1947, nine in the morning, and it is already eighty degrees. The party has been asked, by telephone and by name, to come to the Castellane Pictures lot on Santa Monica Boulevard, through the Gower Street gate where the extras queue, and up to a white bungalow behind the commissary with a lemon tree outside and no name on the door. Inside, Harlan Shay, a soft-spoken, silver-haired man in a beautiful grey suit, pours coffee, lays a studio portrait face up on the desk, and puts five hundred dollars in fifties beside it. The girl in the portrait is Vivian Lark. 'Nine days,' he says. 'She's a good kid from a small town and she's had her head turned by somebody. I'd like her back before the newspapers notice, and before the gentlemen from Washington do. She has a picture opening on the fourth. Find her, tell me where she is, and don't talk to anyone. I'll take it from there.' He smiles. 'I always do.'

setting.name: Los Angeles, 22 September to 4 October 1947
setting.description: The real Los Angeles of 1947, with fictional people moving through it. Hollywood is a few miles of studios, bungalows, drugstores and movie palaces under the hills; the Sunset Strip, the stretch of Sunset Boulevard between Hollywood and Beverly Hills, is unincorporated county land where the Los Angeles Police Department has no jurisdiction and the Sheriff's vice squad can be reasoned with, which is why the nightclubs are there. Downtown is City Hall's white tower, the Hall of Records, the newspaper row, and above it Bunker Hill, a hill of decaying Victorian mansions cut up into rooming houses, reached by the little funicular called Angels Flight. Union Station, eight years old, is the most beautiful building in the city. The Pacific Electric Red Cars still run on the big interurban lines to Santa Monica, Glendale and the Valley, though everyone who can afford a car drives. Santa Monica has the pier, the carousel and the beach. Over the Cahuenga Pass the San Fernando Valley is orange and walnut groves, chicken ranches, movie ranches where the Westerns are shot and the first tract-home developments for veterans. The party works for, and then against, Castellane Pictures, a fictional mid-sized studio founded in 1921 by Bernard Castellane, known on the lot as 'the Castle', which makes Westerns, crime pictures and one prestige picture a year, and is in more financial trouble than anyone outside its accounts department knows. Every person, company, club and studio in this campaign is invented. The committee's hearings, the subpoenas, the housing shortage, the Red Cars and the city's arguments about annexing and watering the Valley are real history.
setting.atmosphere: Hard sunlight and black shadow. Heat that lasts into the night, jacaranda gone to seed, the smell of oranges, gasoline and the sea. The klieg lights and searchlights of premieres sweeping the sky over Hollywood like a war that is still going on somewhere. Cigarettes, whisky, fedoras, nylon stockings that are finally back in the shops, the Dodgers on the radio from Brooklyn, a big band at the Sirocco and a trumpet on Central Avenue. Everyone in this town is selling something and most of them are acting. Play it hard-boiled and humane: the city is corrupt, but the people in it are tired, frightened, funny and trying. Violence is sudden and has consequences: Heat, police, newspapers, a studio that drops you. Competence is the fantasy: let the players feel clever when they read a dead man's swimming pool, find the right clerk at the Hall of Records, or get a doorman to talk with a dollar and a kind word. The committee is the weather over everything. Nobody says the word 'blacklist' out loud yet, but everyone is checking who they had dinner with in 1938.

regions.name: Hollywood and the Castellane Lot
regions.description: Castellane Pictures fills two blocks of Santa Monica Boulevard behind a white wall with a Moorish gate: sound stages like aircraft hangars, the commissary, the stars' bungalows, the transport garage, the writers' building where the typewriters never stop, the nitrate film vault sunk in concrete behind the laboratory, and the back lot, eleven acres of standing sets: a New York street, a Western main street, a European village square, a dry riverbed and a lake that is three feet deep. Studio police patrol it on bicycles. North of the boulevard, Hollywood Boulevard has the movie palaces, the drugstores, the hat-shaped restaurants and the tourists; above it the canyons, Laurel Canyon among them, wind up into the hills where writers and actors live in houses with pools they cannot quite afford.

regions.name: The Sunset Strip
regions.description: A mile and a half of county territory on Sunset Boulevard, outside the city limits, where the nightclubs, the agents' offices and the restaurants for people who want to be seen are. Club Sirocco, owned by Royce Ambler, is the newest and the best: a white Moorish front, a palm court, a bandstand, a dance floor, and upstairs behind a door with no handle a card room where the studio men, the real-estate men and certain members of the city council lose money to each other and are photographed doing it. The Sheriff's vice squad, not the LAPD, polices the Strip, and the Sheriff's men are easier to talk to.

regions.name: Downtown and Bunker Hill
regions.description: City Hall, the Hall of Records and the Hall of Justice, where the coroner's office keeps its cold room in the basement. The newspaper row, where the party's reporter works for the Los Angeles Evening Courier (fictional). Union Station on Alameda Street with its tiled waiting room, leather chairs and lockers. Above Hill Street, Bunker Hill: crumbling Victorian mansions turned into rooming houses for pensioners, waitresses, hopefuls and the broke, reached by the orange-and-black cars of Angels Flight, a penny a ride, or by long concrete stairs. Central Avenue, south of downtown, is the heart of the city's Black community, with its clubs, churches, hotels and Dr. Roland Pryor's clinic.

regions.name: Santa Monica
regions.description: The end of the Red Car line and the end of the continent. The pier, the carousel in its big wooden hippodrome with apartments on the floor above, the bait shops, the fortune tellers, the arcade with the penny photo booth, the fishing boats and the long beach running north toward Malibu and south toward the amusement piers of Ocean Park. Fog comes in at night and the foghorn sounds every thirty seconds.

regions.name: The West Valley
regions.description: Over the Cahuenga Pass and west across the San Fernando Valley: Ventura Boulevard, the Pacific Electric line to Van Nuys, then orange groves in straight dark rows for miles toward Reseda and Chatsworth, packing sheds, irrigation ditches, windbreaks of eucalyptus, chicken ranches, a wrecking yard on Sepulveda, the Castellane movie ranch with its Western town in the rocks, and survey stakes with red flags marching through the groves in lines that do not match any road. The city's water reaches the eastern Valley; the West Valley Tract is outside the line, and whoever gets the mains run out to it will be rich.

campaignRules.name: Heat
campaignRules.description: The party has a single Heat score for Los Angeles, 0 to 10, which the GM tracks openly in the world state and announces every time it changes. Heat measures how much attention the police, the studio, the Sheriff's men, the newspapers and the people who hire killers are paying to the party. It rises: +1 for being seen somewhere you should not be, a blown cover story, or leaning on the wrong man (a councilman, a studio executive, Royce Ambler); +2 for a body found; +2 for a gunshot wound treated at a hospital (they report them); +3 for gunfire in the city limits or on the Strip; +3 for a car chase the police see. It falls by 1 for each full day the party spends quiet (no break-ins, no fights, no leaning). At Heat 3 the cops start asking: a radio car follows the party's car, Lt. Dolan calls them in for a friendly chat. At Heat 6 someone is told to take care of you: Royce Ambler's men or Wendell Haig's professional make an attempt, and the studio stops returning calls. At Heat 9 the city is closed to you: warrants, no hotel will take you, Shay's money stops, and every door the party knocks on is answered by a policeman. Heat starts at 0 in kl-scenario-001.

campaignRules.name: The Calendar
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on a fixed calendar, tracked in the world state with the date and hour. Each day has about five useful scenes (a scene is roughly two hours). Fixed events happen whether or not the party is ready: Mon 22 Sep, Shay hires the party. Tue 23 Sep, Abel Kurland is served a committee subpoena in the morning and dies in his pool that night. Wed 24 Sep, the body is found at 7 a.m. and ruled an accident by noon. Sat 27 Sep, Wendell Haig learns the green ledger is gone and hires Emory Thorne to recover it. Tue 30 Sep, Royce Ambler tries to sell out and is killed unless the party has protected him. Thu 2 Oct, the studio announces that Vivian Lark has returned from a rest cure in Palm Springs and will attend her premiere. Sat 4 Oct, 7 p.m., the premiere of The Gilded Hour at the Pantheon Theatre. Tue 7 Oct, the city council votes on the West Valley annexation and water mains. Mon 20 Oct, the committee's Hollywood hearings open in Washington. Time is what the party spends, and it should feel scarce.

campaignRules.name: Core Clues and the Three-Clue Rule
campaignRules.description: Every conclusion the party needs to reach (each scenario lists them under 'conclusions') has at least three clues in different places. Core clues are found automatically by anyone who looks in the right place with a sensible skill or question: no roll. Rolls only add detail, speed, or a bonus clue, and a failed roll never dead-ends the case; it costs time, Heat or position. The GM should be generous with core clues and stingy with certainty: the clues point, the players conclude. When the players are stuck, use the case board: summarize the suspects, what each one wants, what the party knows, and the open questions, out loud, and ask which lead they want to pull.

campaignRules.name: The Nightly Report
campaignRules.description: Harlan Shay pays the party $50 a day each plus expenses and expects a report by telephone every evening at nine, at his bungalow extension (HEmpstead 2-7700, extension 7). Whatever the party tells Shay, Shay knows, and until the party stops trusting him he acts on it within hours, usually by sending money or a studio policeman ahead of them. Track what Shay knows in the world state. This is not a trick: it is how a fixer works, and it is the best clue in the first half of the campaign. The party that reports on Tuesday evening that Abel Kurland 'knows more than he's saying' has told the man who will be at Kurland's pool at eleven. The party that stops reporting stops the leaks, and Shay notices that too (Heat +1 at the studio, and he tries money: a bonus of $200 each to 'keep me in the loop').

campaignRules.name: Badges, Lines and Prices
campaignRules.description: Los Angeles is a patchwork, and who can arrest you depends on which side of a street you are on. Inside the city limits it is the LAPD; on the Sunset Strip and in unincorporated county land it is the Sheriff; on the Castellane lot it is the studio police, who answer to Harlan Shay. Crossing a line ends a police pursuit more often than speed does. Money moves the city. Rough 1947 prices: a nickel for a payphone, a penny for Angels Flight, a dime for a Red Car fare to Santa Monica, a dollar for a doorman or a parking boy, $5 for a hotel night clerk, $10 for a desk sergeant to look the other way, $20 for a look at a police report, $50 for a coroner's report, $100 to make a deputy forget something, a steak dinner on the Strip $4, a room on Bunker Hill $7 a week, a new Ford $1,300. Every character's money is the dollar figure in their wallet line; change it when they spend.

explorationRules: This is a city campaign and the map is a schematic of the Los Angeles basin: Hollywood in the middle, downtown to the east, the sea to the west, the Valley over the hills to the north. Distance is time. A car across town takes thirty to forty-five minutes; Hollywood to Santa Monica by Red Car is about an hour; over the Cahuenga Pass to the West Valley is an hour by car and most of a morning by Pacific Electric and on foot. The unit of time is the scene, about two hours, and each scenario lists its places as a small sandbox. The opposition acts on its own clock and on what it knows: what Shay has been told, what Ambler's men have seen, what Haig learns from the studio. Narrate the city concretely and fairly: the same tan Chevrolet three cars back on Sunset; a doorman who looks at your shoes before your face; a radio in a drugstore playing a ball game while you wait for a man who is late. Skill checks state a DC and a failure outcome; failures cost time, Heat or position, never the case (see Core Clues). Between scenes let the city breathe: a trumpet from a Central Avenue doorway, the smell of the groves at night, a newsboy shouting about subpoenas, the searchlights over Hollywood every night there is a premiere somewhere. Players should come away knowing what Los Angeles felt like in 1947.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a character's hit points, it does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Every person, company, studio, club and newspaper is fictional. The backdrop is real: the House committee's October 1947 Hollywood hearings and the subpoenas served in September; the postwar housing shortage; the San Fernando Valley's orange groves and the city's water service; the Sunset Strip's county status; Bunker Hill, Angels Flight, Union Station, the Pacific Electric Red Cars and the Santa Monica pier. No real person appears. Real public figures stay off-stage and unnamed.
controlFile.theTruth: Wendell Haig, 58, a Valley real-estate man, has assembled three thousand acres of West Valley orange groves through a company called Encino Verde Land Co. (much of it bought cheap during the war, including the Okada family's grove, sold under duress in 1942 when the family was sent to the Manzanar camp). Outside the city's water service the land is worth $300 an acre as groves; annexed and on the city's water mains, it is worth $3,000 an acre as tract homes for veterans. The council votes on annexation and the mains on Tuesday 7 October. Haig's silent partner, with forty per cent, is Bernard Castellane, whose studio is quietly near bankrupt: he is paying his share, and the bribes, with studio money disguised as $180,000 in location fees to Cahuenga Location Services, Inc., a shell owned by Royce Ambler. Ambler launders the cash through Club Sirocco's card room, where Councilmen Dwight Hollister and Ray Fenwick are allowed to win it at cards, and where Harlan Shay supplies the studio's contract players as dinner companions, and Ambler's hidden camera photographs everyone. Ambler keeps a green ledger of every payment, and the negatives, in his office safe, as insurance against Haig. Councilman Arthur Mabry, the swing vote, refused the money, started asking questions in the groves, and died on Mulholland Drive on the night of 30 August when the brakes of his Buick failed; Haig had hired Emory Thorne, a professional from Chicago, to cut the brake line. Shay, who arranged Thorne's car from the airport as a favour to Haig, does not know what Thorne did, and has been afraid to find out.
controlFile.vivian: Vivian Lark, 24, born Dorothy Ann Pell in Taft, California, was one of the girls Shay sent to the Sirocco. On Saturday 13 September she overheard Haig and Ambler in the corridor say that Mabry had been 'taken care of' and that the next one would be too. She had watched Ambler open his safe often enough to know the combination (his birthday, 4-17-98; she is an actress, she remembers lines). That night she took the green ledger and the envelope of negatives. On Sunday 14 September she gave the negatives to her friend Abel Kurland, the only person at the studio who had ever treated her as an actress, and kept the ledger. Bunny Shearer drove her to Union Station at 9:40 that night; she bought a ticket to Bakersfield in her own name, put a suitcase of studio furs and jewelry in locker 212 as a false trail, did not board, and took the streetcar back to Bunker Hill, where she lived as Dot Pell at Mrs. Gertie Sloane's Alta Vista Rooms. When Ambler's man Tiny Bascombe came asking on Bunker Hill on Saturday 20 September, she moved to the apartment above the Santa Monica carousel that belongs to Marguerite 'Mags' Fennimore, a retired silent-picture actress who was her first landlady in town. She wants Haig and Ambler finished, publicly, by her own hand, and she is willing to burn her own career to do it. Kurland wanted something else: to trade the evidence to Castellane, quietly, for the studio's refusal to give the committee any names, and for the vote to die. They argued about it on the telephone on Monday 22 September.
controlFile.theDeathOfAbelKurland: Abel Kurland, 44, screenwriter, ex-newspaperman, attended meetings of a left-wing writers' group in 1938, and Bernard Castellane, to show the committee the studio is patriotic, has privately agreed to give its investigator, Lyle Preston, his name. Kurland was served a subpoena on Tuesday 23 September, argued with Preston on his own doorstep at six that evening, and at 10:40 p.m. took a call from Shay's office. Shay drove up to Laurel Canyon in his dark green Packard (Castellane lot parking sticker No. 7) at about 11 p.m. with $5,000 in cash from the studio's special-services account to buy the negatives. Kurland laughed at him and told him what they showed, including Shay himself at the Sirocco handing a councilman an envelope. They fought on the pool deck. Kurland swung; Shay hit him, hard, once, and Kurland went backwards and cracked the back of his head on the concrete coping and slid into the deep end. Shay stood at the edge for what he will later say was a minute and was nearer three, while Kurland drowned, because Kurland alive meant the studio, and Shay, finished. Then he searched the house and did not find the negatives (Kurland had put them in the studio nitrate vault on Monday), washed the two glasses and put them in the wrong cupboard, poured the rest of the gin down the sink and left the empty bottle by the pool, wiped it, picked up his money, and drove home. A paper currency band from the $5,000 had blown into the pool and was caught in the skimmer basket. At 12:10 a.m. he telephoned Lt. Frank Dolan at home. Dolan had the case before the pool man found the body at 7 a.m., and Deputy Coroner Walter Ness wrote 'accidental drowning, acute alcoholism' for $200 before the autopsy was finished. Harlan Shay is the client who hired the party. He is not a monster. He is a tired, clever, loyal man who has fixed things for the studio for twenty years and who found out at the edge of a swimming pool what he is.
conclusions: C1 (kl-scenario-001): Vivian left on her own and is hiding, not kidnapped or dead. Clues C1a bungalow, C1b motor-pool log or Bunny, C1c Union Station, C1d bank withdrawal.

C2 (kl-scenario-001): She is living under her birth name, Dorothy Pell. Clues C2a personnel file or Percy, C2b Mrs. Sloane's postcard, C2c locker claim in the name D. Pell, C2d the Angels Flight operator.

C3 (kl-scenario-001): She took something from Club Sirocco and Ambler's men are hunting her. Clues C3a Tiny Bascombe at the Alta Vista, C3b Kurland's fear and the Sirocco card in his study, C3c Ambler's calls to Percy, C3d the Sirocco hat-check girl.
C4 (kl-scenario-001): She is above the Santa Monica carousel. Clues C4a the photo-booth strip, C4b Kurland's answering service, C4c Mags Fennimore through Bunny, Percy or Agnes.
K1 (kl-scenario-002): Kurland was killed, not drunk-drowned. Clues K1a the body, K1b the pool deck, K1c the coroner's report written too early, K1d the page in his typewriter.

K2 (kl-scenario-002, confirmed in 004): Harlan Shay was there and let him drown. Clues K2a sticker No. 7, K2b the answering service, K2c the currency band and the bank, K2d Shay's hand and his slip, K2e Dolan's early call.
K3 (kl-scenario-002): The negatives are in the nitrate vault, can 14. Clues K3a the typewriter page, K3b the message for Dot, K3c the vault key log.
M1 (kl-scenario-003): Studio money is buying councilmen through the Sirocco. Clues M1a the negatives, M1b Cahuenga Location Services, M1c the green ledger, M1d Lew Pardee.

M2 (kl-scenario-003): The money is for Haig's West Valley vote, and Castellane is his partner. Clues M2a the survey stakes and the Okadas, M2b the county recorder, M2c the city engineer's plans, M2d the ledger's partners page.
M3 (kl-scenario-003): Mabry was murdered by a professional Haig hired. Clues M3a Helen Mabry, M3b the brake line in the wrecking yard, M3c the ledger entry 'E.T.', M3d Pardee, M3e Ken Hirano's drive.
P1 (kl-scenario-004): Thorne will shoot Vivian from the searchlight battery on the marquee. Clues P1a the searchlight company's fifth man, P1b Thorne's hotel room, P1c the cue sheet.
redHerrings: Lyle Preston, 38, investigator for the House committee: argued loudly with Kurland at six on the night he died and was seen by neighbours. He wanted names, not a corpse; a dead Kurland is useless to him. He is a careerist, not a killer, and he will try to buy the party's evidence for the committee's purposes.

Tiny Bascombe, Royce Ambler's doorman and muscle: seen in Laurel Canyon on Tuesday afternoon, asking Kurland's maid whether Miss Lark had been visiting. Ambler wanted Kurland alive and talking, because only a living Kurland could lead him to the negatives.

Suicide: the subpoena on Kurland's desk and the gin bottle suggest a frightened man who drank and fell in. The subpoena is unopened, and the page in his typewriter was written at a quarter past eleven by a man who was planning a future.

Vivian herself: she argued with Kurland on the telephone on Monday, and the answering-service operator heard her say 'Then I'll do it without you.' She was above the Santa Monica carousel with the party, or with Mags Fennimore, at the time he died.
controlFile.outcomes: History is not changed: the committee's hearings open on 20 October whatever happens, and the city keeps growing. The party decides what happens to the green ledger, the negatives and Harlan Shay. The main roads, which the GM should present honestly in kl-scenario-004: (1) Give it to the newspapers or say it into the radio microphone at the premiere: Haig and Ambler (if alive) are indicted, the West Valley vote dies, Hollister and Fenwick resign, Castellane Pictures collapses into receivership and six hundred people lose their jobs, Vivian's career ends with her photograph on every front page beside a councilman, and Lyle Preston uses the scandal to call the studio a nest of subversives and names Abel Kurland in the hearings anyway. (2) Give it to Preston: he promises to see justice done and instead uses it to make Bernard Castellane name thirty people to the committee; the vote passes; the party is safe and owed a favour by Washington. (3) Sell it back: Castellane will pay $25,000, Haig $40,000; nothing changes, and Thorne is still alive. (4) Use it as a quiet lever: force Castellane to refuse the committee and withdraw from the syndicate, make Hollister and Fenwick vote no, make Haig return the Okada grove; nobody goes to prison, Mabry's and Kurland's deaths stay accidents, and the party holds a loaded gun over the city for the rest of their lives (permanent Heat 3, and the city's powerful know their names). Harlan Shay can be turned in to the District Attorney's office with the K2 clues (manslaughter, and he will plead), let go, used as a witness against Haig in exchange for leniency, or allowed to make his own confession at the microphone. Vivian has her own preference, road 1 under her own name; the party can help her, persuade her, or overrule her, and she will remember which.
